items.snippet: Start with the valuation logic. Historically, a talent-heavy R&D engine scaled r...
items.raw_snippet:
Start with the valuation logic. Historically, a talent-heavy R&D engine scaled roughly in line with headcount. To do twice the research, a company generally needed twice the researchers. Operating leverage was modest, and margin expansion came from scaling go-to-market activities or improving gross margins, not from making R&D itself more efficient.

AI should upend that assumption. [...] Of all the analytical doors DISE opens, the one most likely to surprise people is the talent-versus-infrastructure split inside R&D. This distinction has always been an interesting question with meaningful valuation implications. Now, as artificial intelligence changes labor force productivity, the story told by the numbers will evolve markedly. [...] The distinction is important because, relative to ABC, XYZ has a more infrastructure-intensive R&D engine. Investors will view that as a sign of lower SBC dilution risk and more stable cash compensation, but also a slower path to operating leverage on the R&D line. The valuation conversation may pivot toward whether XYZ is investing enough in talent, particularly engineering talent capable of competing in an AI-native landscape, relative to peers carrying higher SBC ratios. items.title: AGILOX Tech Talk Why Physical AI Changes Manufacturing
items.snippet: For 250 years, industrial progress has followed a remarkably consistent pattern:...
items.raw_snippet:
For 250 years, industrial progress has followed a remarkably consistent pattern: we have found new ways to amplify human capabilities. First muscle, then efficiency, then reliability, then connectivity. Now, we are entering the next chapter – intelligence. David Niedermayier, Co-CEO and Co-Founder of AGILOX, explores what happens when AI moves from our screens into machines, and why this shift could become critical for the future of European manufacturing. [...] By David Niedermaier, Co-CEO & Co-Founder, AGILOX

When we talk about smart manufacturing, we tend to think immediately about robots, autonomous systems and increasingly sophisticated machines. But before looking at where manufacturing is heading, I think it is worth taking a step back, because what we are experiencing today is not an isolated technological development. It is part of a much bigger story –- one that began around 250 years ago with the Industrial Revolution. [...] Then came Industry 4.0. We connected machines to one another and connected factories to the digital world. Data became an increasingly important resource, allowing us to monitor processes, optimize operations and understand production in ways that had not previously been possible.

And now we are entering another chapter.

The chapter of intelligence.

AI is beginning to move from the screen into the machine, and that shift has implications that go far beyond technology itself.
